title: A tiny health check
prompt: Implement healthCode() to return the integer 200. The test harness supplies main(); your file only needs the function.
hints: Declare an int return type and use a return statement.
explanation: C++ needs a declared return type. The compiler turns this function into native code before it can run.
starter: int healthCode() { return 0; }

title: Count the pages
prompt: Implement pageCount(items, perPage) for nonnegative item counts and positive page sizes. Include a partially filled final page. Inputs are at most 10,000.
hints: Integer division discards the remainder. Add one page if the remainder is nonzero.
explanation: Both operands being int means division produces an int. The % operator lets you detect the leftover items.
starter: int pageCount(int items, int perPage) { return 0; }

title: Initialize the retry budget
prompt: Inside retryBudget(), declare an int named retries, value-initialize it with {}, then add 3 and return it. Why would int retries; be unsafe here?
hints: Empty braces initialize an int to zero.
explanation: An automatic int declared without an initializer has an indeterminate value. Reading that value is undefined behavior in C++20. Empty braces value-initialize an int to zero, so adding to it starts from a known value.
starter: int retryBudget() { /* TODO */ return -1; }

title: Keep the fractional seconds
prompt: Implement seconds(milliseconds) returning double. Preserve the fraction: 1250 ms is 1.25 seconds. Inputs are nonnegative.
hints: Convert before dividing, or use a floating-point divisor.
explanation: Converting an already-truncated integer result to double cannot restore the fraction. Operand types determine how the expression is evaluated.
starter: double seconds(int milliseconds) { return milliseconds / 1000; }

title: A copy of the counter
prompt: Implement bumped(int counter) returning counter + 1. In a separate scratch program, call it with a local variable and verify the original is unchanged.
hints: The parameter is a separate int object initialized from the argument.
explanation: Passing an int by value copies the value. Changing the parameter does not assign to the caller’s variable.
starter: int bumped(int counter) { return counter; }

title: A compile-time upload limit
prompt: Define constexpr int maxUploadKiB as 2048. Implement fitsUpload(int kib) for the inclusive range 0..maxUploadKiB. Explain why constexpr is stronger than const.
hints: A constexpr variable must have a constant-expression initializer.
explanation: const prevents modification of an initialized variable. constexpr also requires a constant-expression initializer, allowing the value to be used where the compiler requires a compile-time constant.
starter:
// TODO: maxUploadKiB
bool fitsUpload(int kib) { return false; }

title: Build a route
prompt: Implement route(std::string name) returning /api/ followed by name. Empty name should return /api/. Include the header you use.
hints: Use a std::string for the prefix; + concatenates strings.
explanation: std::string owns its characters and can grow. A string literal is not itself a std::string object.
starter:
#include <string>
std::string route(std::string name) { return name; }

title: An access rule
prompt: Implement canPublish(isAdmin, isOwner, isLocked): an admin or owner may publish, but nobody may publish a locked item.
hints: Group the admin-or-owner condition before combining it with the lock check.
explanation: Parentheses make the intended grouping explicit. && binds more tightly than ||, which can make an ungrouped rule accidentally allow admins through the lock.
starter: bool canPublish(bool isAdmin, bool isOwner, bool isLocked) { return false; }
tests: for (bool a : {false,true}) for (bool o : {false,true}) for (bool l : {false,true}) assert(canPublish(a,o,l) == ((a || o) && !l));

title: Avoid a shadowed result
prompt: Fix status(bool ok) so it returns 200 on success and 503 otherwise. The inner declaration currently hides the outer variable.
hints: Assign to the existing result instead of declaring another int.
explanation: A nested declaration can reuse a name while referring to a different object. Updating that inner object does not change the outer one.
starter: int status(bool ok) { int result{503}; if (ok) { int result{200}; } return result; }

title: Two timeout policies
prompt: Define timeout() in namespaces api and worker. Return 30 from api::timeout() and 120 from worker::timeout().
hints: Put each function inside namespace name { ... }.
explanation: Namespaces distinguish otherwise identical names. Use :: to select a namespace member; this is not object property access.
starter: // TODO: two namespaces and their timeout functions

title: Classify a response
prompt: Implement category(int code): return 2 for 200 or 201, 4 for 400 or 404, and 0 otherwise. Practise using switch.
hints: Several case labels can share the same return statement.
explanation: A return exits the function, so these cases need no break. Without return or break, control continues into the next case.
starter: int category(int code) { return 0; }

title: Total the retry delays
prompt: Implement totalDelay(int attempts): delays are 1, 2, ..., attempts seconds. Return their sum using a loop. attempts is in 0..100.
hints: Initialize an accumulator to zero, and include the final attempt.
explanation: A loop condition is evaluated before each iteration. For zero attempts, the body should not execute.
starter: int totalDelay(int attempts) { return 0; }

title: Guard a bounded value
prompt: Implement clampPercent(int value), clamping integers to 0..100. Add your own assertions for values just inside and outside both boundaries.
hints: Check below zero first, then above 100, otherwise keep the original value.
explanation: Boundary tests distinguish < from <= mistakes and catch accidental changes to valid input. Assertions test assumptions; they are not a substitute for validating user input.
starter: int clampPercent(int value) { return value; }
tests: assert(clampPercent(-1)==0); assert(clampPercent(0)==0); assert(clampPercent(1)==1); assert(clampPercent(99)==99); assert(clampPercent(100)==100); assert(clampPercent(101)==100);

title: Compute a success ratio
prompt: Implement ratio(int success, int total), returning double. Return 0.0 when total is zero; otherwise return the fractional quotient. Inputs satisfy 0 <= success <= total.
hints: Guard zero, then cast an operand before division.
explanation: Casts make a conversion explicit. A double return type alone does not make an integer division floating-point.
starter: double ratio(int success, int total) { return 0.0; }

title: What does auto deduce?
prompt: Define auto batchSize initialized from 16 and auto retrySeconds initialized from 0.5. Implement auto nextBatch() to return batchSize + 1. Predict each deduced type before checking.
hints: auto deduces from the initializer expression, not future assignments.
explanation: auto asks the compiler to deduce a type from the initializer. The resulting variable still has a fixed type. Integer and floating-point literals therefore lead to different deduced types.
starter: // TODO: batchSize, retrySeconds and nextBatch()

title: One name, two payload types
prompt: Define payloadSize(int) returning sizeof(int) as an int, and payloadSize(std::string) returning the string length as an int. Include <string>. Test both overloads.
hints: The parameter types must differ; changing only the return type cannot create an overload.
explanation: Overloads are distinct functions with the same name and different parameter lists. The compiler selects an overload from the argument types. A different return type alone cannot distinguish two overloads.
starter:
#include <string>
// TODO: payloadSize overloads

title: Resolve the numeric overload
prompt: Define pick(int) returning 1 and pick(double) returning 2. Implement pickHalf() calling pick with 0.5. Predict what pick(1.0f) selects.
hints: float promotes to double; an exact match beats a conversion.
explanation: The compiler ranks viable overloads. An explicit cast can make your intended argument type clear when a call would otherwise be ambiguous.
starter: // TODO: pick overloads and pickHalf()

title: A default retry allowance
prompt: Implement retryWindow(int delay, int attempts = 3), returning delay * attempts. Inputs are nonnegative and at most 100. Call it with one and two arguments.
hints: Place the default on the trailing parameter.
explanation: A missing argument is supplied from the default at the call site. Adding a one-parameter overload as well would make one-argument calls ambiguous here.
starter: // TODO: retryWindow

title: Convert a temperature
prompt: Implement fahrenheit(double celsius) using F = C × 9/5 + 32. Preserve fractional results. Inputs are within -100..100.
hints: Use floating-point operands for the conversion factor.
explanation: Integer division happens before multiplication when parenthesized as (9 / 5). Floating-point literals preserve the fractional scale factor.

title: Extract whole minutes
prompt: Implement wholeMinutes(int seconds) for 0..100000 seconds. Discard any incomplete minute.
hints: Integer division already truncates a nonnegative quotient.
explanation: For nonnegative integers, division gives the number of complete groups. The remainder can be handled separately when needed.

title: Extract remaining seconds
prompt: Implement remainingSeconds(int seconds): return seconds left after removing whole minutes. Inputs are 0..100000.
hints: The remainder operator is %.
explanation: For positive divisors and nonnegative dividends, the remainder lies between zero and one less than the divisor.

title: Recognize even numbers
prompt: Implement isEven(int n), including negative numbers and zero.
hints: A number is even when its remainder after division by 2 is zero.
explanation: Testing equality to zero works for positive and negative even integers. Do not assume every nonzero remainder is positive.

title: Return a sign
prompt: Implement signOf(int value) returning -1, 0, or 1 for negative, zero, or positive values. Avoid negating the input.
hints: Compare against zero rather than calculating an absolute value.
explanation: Comparisons are safe even for the minimum representable int. Negating that minimum would overflow.

title: Check an inclusive interval
prompt: Implement inRange(int x, int low, int high). Return true only when low <= x <= high; an inverted interval contains nothing.
hints: Combine two comparisons with &&.
explanation: A chained comparison such as low <= x <= high does not express an interval test in C++. The first comparison produces bool, which would then be compared to high.

title: Widen before multiplying
prompt: Implement area(int width, int height) returning long long. Inputs are nonnegative and at most 100000; the product may exceed int.
hints: Convert an operand before multiplication.
explanation: The multiplication type is determined by its operands, not the return type. Widening before the operation avoids signed int overflow.

title: Round up without addition overflow
prompt: Implement groups(int count, int size) for nonnegative count and positive size. Return ceiling(count/size), including for count equal to INT_MAX.
hints: Use quotient plus a nonzero-remainder check instead of count + size - 1.
explanation: Algebraically equivalent formulas can have different overflow behavior in fixed-width integer arithmetic. A quotient/remainder formulation avoids the large intermediate sum.

title: Read a decimal digit
prompt: Implement digitValue(char c) returning 0..9 for ASCII digit characters and -1 otherwise.
hints: Check the range before subtracting the character zero.
explanation: A char holds a character code. Decimal digit codes are contiguous, so subtraction yields the numeric value after validation.

title: Compare approximate values
prompt: Implement near(double a, double b, double tolerance), true when the absolute difference is <= tolerance. Inputs are finite and tolerance is nonnegative.
hints: Use std::abs from <cmath>.
explanation: Rounding makes exact floating-point equality unsuitable for many computed values. An absolute tolerance describes an acceptable error in the units being measured.

title: Select the smaller value
prompt: Implement smaller(int a, int b) using the conditional operator. Equal values should be returned unchanged.
hints: The form is condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse.
explanation: The conditional operator is an expression: it selects and yields one branch value. Only the selected branch is evaluated.

title: Test a bit flag
prompt: Implement hasFlag(unsigned value, unsigned mask), true when all bits in mask are set in value. A zero mask should return true.
hints: Compare value & mask with mask.
explanation: Bitwise AND keeps only bits present in both operands. Comparing the masked value with the mask tests every requested bit.

title: Join two labels
prompt: Implement joinLabels(std::string a, std::string b), joining nonempty labels with one space. If either is empty, return the other unchanged.
hints: Handle empty strings before concatenating.
explanation: Empty strings are valid values. Explicit handling prevents separators at the beginning or end of the result.

title: Safely read the first character
prompt: Implement firstOr(std::string text, char fallback), returning the first character or fallback when empty.
hints: Check empty() before indexing.
explanation: A string has no first character when its size is zero. Validate the index before accessing an element.

title: Count a character
prompt: Implement countChar(std::string text, char target). Count every matching character. Inputs contain at most 1000 characters.
hints: Use a range-based for loop over the characters.
explanation: A range-based loop visits each element without manual indexing. Initialize the count before the loop so empty input produces zero.

title: Check a prefix
prompt: Implement startsWith(std::string text, std::string prefix) using C++20 starts_with(). Empty prefix always matches.
hints: std::string::starts_with accepts another string.
explanation: A prefix comparison begins at position zero and does not change the string. An empty prefix matches because it requires no characters.

title: Check a suffix
prompt: Implement endsWith(std::string text, std::string suffix) using C++20 ends_with(). Empty suffix always matches.
hints: Use the corresponding suffix member function.
explanation: Suffix checks compare the final characters without allocating a substring. The suffix must fit within the original string.

title: Replace characters in a copy
prompt: Implement replaced(std::string text, char from, char to). Return a copy with every occurrence replaced. Do not modify the caller’s string.
hints: Iterate with char& to modify each character of the local copy.
explanation: The string parameter is passed by value, so its characters belong to a separate string. References in the loop modify that local string.
tests: std::string s{"a-b-c"}; assert(replaced(s,'-',' ')=="a b c"); assert(s=="a-b-c"); assert(replaced("",'a','b').empty());

title: Take a non-owning prefix
prompt: Implement head(std::string_view text, std::size_t n), returning a view of its first n characters, or all of it when n is larger. The caller keeps the source alive.
hints: substr(0, n) truncates a count that exceeds the remaining length.
explanation: string_view refers to existing characters and does not own them. Returning a view is safe only while the referenced storage remains alive.
tests: std::string s{"orchard"}; auto v=head(s,3); assert(v=="orc"); assert(v.data()==s.data()); assert(head(s,99)==s); assert(head(s,0).empty());

title: Turn a view into owned text
prompt: Implement owned(std::string_view text), returning an independent std::string. It must remain unchanged if the source is later modified.
hints: Construct a std::string explicitly from the view.
explanation: Converting a view to a string copies the characters. The resulting string owns its storage and no longer depends on the source’s lifetime.
tests: std::string source{"maple"}; auto copy=owned(source); source[0]='M'; assert(copy=="maple"); assert(owned("").empty());

title: Multiply a small integer power
prompt: Implement power(int base, int exponent) for base -5..5 and exponent 0..8. Return 1 for exponent zero, including 0^0 for this task.
hints: Start with the multiplicative identity, 1.
explanation: An accumulator’s initial value determines the empty-loop result. Multiplication uses 1 as its identity, while addition uses 0.

title: Compute a bounded factorial
prompt: Implement factorial(int n) for n in 0..12. Return n!, with 0! equal to 1.
hints: Multiply the integers from 2 through n.
explanation: The input bound keeps the result within a 32-bit signed int. Numeric algorithms need explicit bounds when using fixed-width types.

title: Sum decimal digits
prompt: Implement digitSum(unsigned n). Repeatedly extract decimal digits and return their sum. Zero should produce zero.
hints: Use % 10 to read a digit and / 10 to remove it.
explanation: Integer division reduces the remaining number each iteration. This gives the loop a termination argument: a positive value eventually reaches zero.

title: Count digits including zero
prompt: Implement digitCount(unsigned n). Zero has one decimal digit. Use a do-while loop.
hints: Count once before testing the remaining value.
explanation: A do-while loop executes at least once. That fits a representation where even zero occupies one digit.

title: Use Euclid’s algorithm
prompt: Implement gcd(unsigned a, unsigned b). Return their greatest common divisor; define gcd(0,0) as zero.
hints: Replace (a,b) with (b,a%b) until b becomes zero.
explanation: Remainders preserve the common divisors while reducing the problem. Save the remainder before overwriting either operand.

title: Stop at the square root
prompt: Implement isPrime(int n) for 0..1000000. Return false below 2. Stop testing divisors once d > n/d.
hints: If a factor exceeds the square root, its paired factor is smaller.
explanation: A failed divisibility test can return immediately. Comparing d <= n/d avoids a potentially overflowing d*d expression.
tests: assert(!isPrime(0)); assert(!isPrime(1)); assert(isPrime(2)); assert(!isPrime(49)); assert(isPrime(97)); assert(!isPrime(1000000));

title: Reverse decimal digits
prompt: Implement reversedDigits(unsigned n) for n <= 1000000. Leading zeros in the reversed result disappear.
hints: Shift the accumulated result by one decimal place before appending a digit.
explanation: Multiplying by ten and adding the next digit constructs a decimal number. A numeric result cannot preserve leading zeros.

title: Keep only the previous two values
prompt: Implement fibonacci(int n) for 0..30, with F0=0 and F1=1. Use a loop and constant extra storage.
hints: Track consecutive values and save their sum before shifting them.
explanation: When a recurrence depends only on two previous values, the full sequence need not be stored. Update order matters because assignments replace old values.

title: Skip unwanted values
prompt: Implement sumWithoutMultiples(int n, int divisor), summing 1..n except multiples of divisor. n is 0..100 and divisor is positive. Practise continue.
hints: Use continue when i % divisor is zero.
explanation: continue skips the rest of the current iteration. In a for loop, the iteration expression still runs before the condition is checked again.

title: Count set bits
prompt: Implement bitCount(unsigned n) using shifts and a loop. Return the number of one bits.
hints: Inspect the low bit with & 1u, then shift right.
explanation: Unsigned right shifts insert zeros. Repeated shifts therefore terminate even when the highest bit was originally set.

title: Declare before calling
prompt: Define int twice(int) and int fourTimes(int). Place fourTimes before twice in the file and use a forward declaration so fourTimes can call twice twice. Inputs are -100..100.
hints: A declaration states the signature without providing the body.
explanation: A function name must be declared before it is used. A forward declaration lets definitions be arranged independently of the call order.

title: Overload by parameter count
prompt: Define volume(int side) for a cube, and volume(int w,int h,int d) for a box. Dimensions are 0..100.
hints: Overloads can differ in the number of parameters.
explanation: The number of arguments helps determine which overload is viable. Both functions can return the same type and still provide distinct interfaces.
starter: // TODO: define the one-argument and three-argument volume overloads.

title: Give a trailing parameter a default
prompt: Implement advance(int position,int step=1). Return position + step. Both inputs are within -1000..1000.
hints: Put the default in the function declaration or definition, not both.
explanation: Default arguments let callers omit trailing arguments. They do not create additional function overloads.

title: Square two numeric types
prompt: Define template<typename T> T square(T value), supporting int and double. Test that the return type matches the argument type. Values are small enough to avoid overflow.
hints: Use the template type for both the parameter and result.
explanation: A function template describes a family of functions. The compiler instantiates a version for each required type.

title: Choose a maximum generically
prompt: Define template<typename T> T maximum(T a,T b) for comparable values of the same type. Return a on a tie.
hints: Only operator< is required to compare the two values.
explanation: Using one template parameter requires a consistent deduced argument type. The function can support strings as well as arithmetic values if comparison is defined.

title: Deduce a result from an expression
prompt: Define template<typename A,typename B> auto sum(A a,B b), returning a+b. Support int and double combinations. Values are within -100..100.
hints: Use different template parameters so each argument can have its own type.
explanation: The return expression determines an auto return type. Arithmetic conversion rules decide the type of a+b.

title: Use a non-type template parameter
prompt: Define template<int Factor> int scaled(int value), multiplying by Factor. Factor and value are within -100..100.
hints: Factor is available as a compile-time value inside the function.
explanation: A non-type template parameter supplies a value as part of an instantiation. Different factors select different template instantiations.

title: Evaluate a function at compile time
prompt: Implement constexpr int triangle(int n) summing 1..n for n in 0..100. Make it usable in static_assert.
hints: A constexpr function can contain a loop in C++20.
explanation: constexpr permits a function call to be evaluated as a constant expression when the arguments and execution satisfy the requirements. The function can still be called at runtime.

title: Retain a local value between calls
prompt: Implement nextId() returning 1,2,3,... on successive calls in one program. Use a static local int initialized to zero.
hints: A static local variable survives function returns.
explanation: A static local has block scope but static storage duration. Initialization happens once, so subsequent calls reuse the stored value.

title: Name a distance type
prompt: Define using Distance = long long, then implement Distance combined(Distance a,Distance b). Inputs are 0..10 billion.
hints: A type alias gives an existing type another name.
explanation: Aliases improve the meaning of declarations but do not create distinct types. Distance and long long remain the same type.
starter: // TODO: declare Distance, then define combined.

title: Change the caller’s value
prompt: Implement void increment(int& value), increasing the caller’s value by one. Input is within -1000..1000.
hints: A reference parameter is an alias for the argument.
explanation: Assignments through a non-const lvalue reference affect the referenced object. No second int is created for the parameter.
tests: int n{7}; increment(n); assert(n==8); increment(n); assert(n==9);

title: Swap two objects
prompt: Implement void swapValues(int& a,int& b) using a temporary. It must also work if both references name the same object.
hints: Save a before assigning b into it.
explanation: References can alias the same object. A temporary preserves the original value and makes a self-swap harmless.
tests: int a=2,b=9; swapValues(a,b); assert(a==9 && b==2); swapValues(a,a); assert(a==9);

title: Read a string without copying
prompt: Implement std::size_t lengthOf(const std::string& text). Return its length without modifying it or copying the whole string.
hints: A const reference permits reading but not modification through that reference.
explanation: Binding a const reference avoids a by-value copy. The const qualifier documents that this function will not modify the argument through the parameter.
tests: const std::string s{"birch"}; assert(lengthOf(s)==5); assert(lengthOf("")==0); static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(&lengthOf),std::size_t(*)(const std::string&)>);

title: Read an optional address
prompt: Implement readOr(const int* value,int fallback). Return *value for a non-null pointer, otherwise fallback.
hints: Test the pointer before dereferencing it.
explanation: nullptr represents the absence of an address. Dereferencing it is invalid, so nullable pointer APIs need an explicit absent case.
tests: int n=12; assert(readOr(&n,-1)==12); assert(readOr(nullptr,-1)==-1); n=0; assert(readOr(&n,9)==0);

title: Update through a pointer
prompt: Implement setIfPresent(int* target,int value), assigning through target when non-null. Null is a no-op.
hints: Use *target on the left of assignment after a null check.
explanation: The pointer parameter itself is copied, but both copies can point to the same int. Dereferencing changes that shared object.
tests: int n=3; setIfPresent(&n,8); assert(n==8); setIfPresent(nullptr,99); assert(n==8);

title: Return an alias to the larger object
prompt: Implement int& largerRef(int& a,int& b), returning a reference to the larger value, or a on a tie. Never return a local temporary.
hints: Return one of the reference parameters directly.
explanation: A returned reference must refer to an object that outlives the call. References to caller-owned arguments meet that requirement while local variables do not.
tests: int a=2,b=7; largerRef(a,b)=10; assert(b==10 && a==2); a=10; assert(&largerRef(a,b)==&a);

title: Report a division result
prompt: Implement bool divide(int numerator,int denominator,int& result). Return false on a zero denominator and leave result unchanged; otherwise store the integer quotient and return true. Inputs are -1000..1000.
hints: Validate first, then assign the output.
explanation: An output reference lets the function return a value separately from its success flag. On failure, preserving the output avoids an unexpected partial update.
tests: int out=99; assert(!divide(4,0,out)); assert(out==99); assert(divide(9,2,out)); assert(out==4); assert(divide(-9,2,out)); assert(out==-4);

title: Represent a missing result
prompt: Implement std::optional<int> quotient(int a,int b), returning nullopt when b is zero. Inputs are -1000..1000.
hints: Return a normal int on success; optional can hold it.
explanation: optional represents either a value or no value. Unlike a sentinel integer, the empty state cannot be confused with a valid numerical result.

title: Choose an optional fallback
prompt: Implement int resolved(std::optional<int> value,int fallback) using value_or. A stored zero must not trigger the fallback.
hints: Test presence, not the truthiness of the contained integer.
explanation: An optional containing zero is engaged. Presence and the stored value are separate pieces of information.

title: Detect whether references alias
prompt: Implement bool sameObject(const int& a,const int& b), comparing object identity rather than values.
hints: Take each reference’s address with &.
explanation: Two distinct objects can contain equal values. Comparing addresses distinguishes identity from equality of contents.
tests: int a=5,b=5; assert(sameObject(a,a)); assert(!sameObject(a,b)); const int& alias=a; assert(sameObject(alias,a));

title: Return an aggregate
prompt: Define struct Point with int x and y, both defaulting to zero. Implement Point shifted(Point p,int dx,int dy), returning the translated point. Values are within -1000..1000.
hints: Access fields with the dot operator.
explanation: A struct groups related values. Passing it by value gives the function its own copy, so returning a modified copy leaves the input object unchanged.
starter:
struct Point { /* TODO: x and y */ };
// TODO: shifted
tests: Point origin{}; assert(origin.x==0 && origin.y==0); Point p{2,3}; auto q=shifted(p,-1,4); assert(q.x==1 && q.y==7); assert(p.x==2 && p.y==3);

title: Give a value a member function
prompt: Define struct Rectangle with int width and height defaulting to zero, and int area() const. Dimensions are 0..100.
hints: The member function can read width and height directly.
explanation: A member function operates on a particular object. Marking a read-only operation const allows calls on const objects.
starter: struct Rectangle { int width{}; int height{}; int area() const; };

title: Name a finite set of states
prompt: Define enum class Direction { north,east,south,west }; implement Direction opposite(Direction d).
hints: Use a switch over scoped enumerator names.
explanation: A scoped enum keeps enumerator names inside its type and does not implicitly convert to int. This helps prevent mixing unrelated categories.
starter:
enum class Direction { north,east,south,west };
Direction opposite(Direction d);

title: Provide member defaults
prompt: Define struct Settings with int attempts=3 and bool verbose=false. Implement Settings quietOnce(), returning attempts=1 and verbose=false.
hints: Default member initializers apply to members omitted from aggregate initialization.
explanation: Member defaults keep useful initial values near the declaration. Aggregate initialization can override selected leading members.
starter:
struct Settings { /* TODO: defaults */ };
Settings quietOnce();
tests: Settings s{}; assert(s.attempts==3 && !s.verbose); auto q=quietOnce(); assert(q.attempts==1 && !q.verbose);

title: Protect a counter’s state
prompt: Define class Counter with private int state starting at zero; public void increment() and int value() const.
hints: Place the data member before public: or explicitly mark it private.
explanation: Private data prevents callers from bypassing the class’s operations. Public member functions expose the behavior the type supports.
starter: class Counter { int count{}; public: void increment(); int value() const; };
tests: Counter c; assert(c.value()==0); c.increment(); c.increment(); assert(c.value()==2); const Counter copy=c; assert(copy.value()==2);

title: Initialize members in a constructor
prompt: Define class Interval with private int low and high, constructor Interval(int,int), and int width() const returning high-low. Inputs satisfy -1000 <= low <= high <= 1000.
hints: Use the constructor’s member initializer list.
explanation: Member initializer lists initialize members before the constructor body runs. This differs from assigning new values after default initialization.
starter: class Interval { int low; int high; public: Interval(int a,int b); int width() const; };

title: Require an explicit unit conversion
prompt: Define class Metres with an explicit constructor from double and double value() const. Store the supplied value unchanged.
hints: Prefix the constructor with explicit.
explanation: explicit prevents implicit conversion through a constructor. Callers must state when a raw number should become a value of the wrapper type.
starter: class Metres { double amount; public: /* TODO: constructor */ double value() const; };

title: Store a generic value
prompt: Define template<typename T> struct Box containing T value{}, plus T get() const returning a copy.
hints: The member type uses the class template parameter.
explanation: A class template generates a distinct type for each template argument. Box<int> and Box<std::string> therefore store different types safely.
starter:
#include <string>
template<typename T> struct Box { /* TODO: value and get */ };
tests: Box<int> a{7}; assert(a.get()==7); const Box<std::string> b{"elm"}; assert(b.get()=="elm"); assert(Box<int>{}.get()==0);

title: Preserve value semantics
prompt: Define struct Label containing std::string text and void rename(std::string next). A copied Label must keep independent text when the original changes.
hints: Let std::string’s normal copy behavior manage its storage.
explanation: Members such as std::string already implement copying and destruction. The compiler-generated operations compose those behaviors without manual memory management.
starter:
#include <string>
struct Label { std::string text; void rename(std::string next); };
tests: Label a{"cedar"}; Label b=a; a.rename("pine"); assert(a.text=="pine"); assert(b.text=="cedar");

title: Maintain an invariant
prompt: Define class Percentage with a default value of 0, void set(int), and int value() const. Clamp every assigned value to 0..100 using private storage.
hints: Keep validation in set so every public update follows the same rule.
explanation: An invariant is a condition the type keeps true. Private storage and a validating setter prevent invalid states through the public interface.
starter: class Percentage { int current{}; public: void set(int n); int value() const; };
tests: Percentage p; assert(p.value()==0); p.set(40); assert(p.value()==40); p.set(-1); assert(p.value()==0); p.set(101); assert(p.value()==100);

title: Sum a collection
prompt: Implement int total(const std::vector<int>& values). Empty input produces zero. At most 100 values, each within -1000..1000.
hints: Use a const-reference parameter and a range-based loop.
explanation: A vector manages a sequence whose size can vary at runtime. Passing it by const reference avoids copying the sequence for a read-only operation.

title: Build a filtered vector
prompt: Implement std::vector<int> positives(const std::vector<int>& values). Keep only values greater than zero, in original order.
hints: Append matching values with push_back.
explanation: Returning a vector by value is a natural ownership transfer. The caller receives an independent result containing just the selected elements.

title: Represent an empty collection result
prompt: Implement std::optional<int> largest(const std::vector<int>& values). Return nullopt when empty and the largest element otherwise.
hints: Initialize from the first element rather than zero.
explanation: Zero is not a valid initial maximum for a collection containing only negative values. The first element gives a valid starting candidate, and optional represents empty input.

title: Double each element
prompt: Implement void doubleAll(std::vector<int>& values), doubling every element in place. Elements are within -1000..1000.
hints: Use int& as the loop variable.
explanation: A by-value range variable is a copy. A reference range variable aliases each element so assignments update the vector.
tests: std::vector<int> v{1,-2,0}; doubleAll(v); assert((v==std::vector<int>{2,-4,0})); std::vector<int> e; doubleAll(e); assert(e.empty());

title: Extend with zeros
prompt: Implement void extend(std::vector<int>& values,std::size_t minimum). Grow to minimum with zero-valued new elements, but never shrink. minimum is at most 1000.
hints: Call resize only if size is below the minimum.
explanation: resize changes the number of elements; reserve changes capacity without adding elements. Value-initialized int elements are zero.
tests: std::vector<int> v{4,5}; extend(v,4); assert((v==std::vector<int>{4,5,0,0})); extend(v,1); assert(v.size()==4);

title: Pop only when nonempty
prompt: Implement std::optional<int> popLast(std::vector<int>& values). Remove and return the last value, or nullopt when empty.
hints: Save back() before calling pop_back().
explanation: pop_back removes an element without returning it. Reading and removing are separate operations, and both require a nonempty vector.
tests: std::vector<int> v{2,5}; assert(*popLast(v)==5); assert((v==std::vector<int>{2})); assert(*popLast(v)==2); assert(!popLast(v));

title: Multiply corresponding components
prompt: Implement int dot(const std::array<int,3>& a,const std::array<int,3>& b), summing a[i]*b[i]. Components are within -100..100.
hints: The arrays have exactly three elements.
explanation: std::array stores its size in the type. A dot product combines corresponding elements and accumulates their products.

title: Return a reversed fixed-size array
prompt: Implement std::array<int,4> reversed(std::array<int,4> values). Return the elements in reverse order.
hints: Swap the first with the last and the second with the third.
explanation: Passing a small fixed-size array by value makes an independent copy. Returning that copy leaves the caller’s array unchanged.

title: Accumulate a running total
prompt: Implement std::vector<int> runningTotals(const std::vector<int>& values). Each result element is the sum up to that position. At most 100 elements within -1000..1000.
hints: Maintain a running sum and append it after every addition.
explanation: The running accumulator is state carried from one loop iteration to the next. The result must have the same length as the input.

title: Collapse neighboring duplicates
prompt: Implement std::vector<int> collapse(const std::vector<int>& values), retaining only one value from each consecutive equal run. Do not remove separated duplicates.
hints: Append if the result is empty or its last value differs.
explanation: Consecutive duplication is different from global duplication. Tracking the most recently emitted value preserves order and later occurrences.

title: Check an index before access
prompt: Implement std::optional<int> atOrNone(const std::vector<int>& values,int index). Reject negative and out-of-range indices.
hints: Check negativity before converting to the unsigned size type.
explanation: Vector sizes are unsigned. Validating the signed index first avoids misleading signed/unsigned comparisons and invalid indexing.

title: Read a nested fixed-size array
prompt: Implement int trace(const std::array<std::array<int,3>,3>& matrix), summing the main diagonal. Elements are within -1000..1000.
hints: For the main diagonal, row and column indices are equal.
explanation: A nested array stores rows as its elements. Two subscripts first select a row and then an element within that row.

title: Sort without changing the source
prompt: Implement std::vector<int> sorted(std::vector<int> values) using std::sort. Return ascending order.
hints: Sort the local copy from begin() to end().
explanation: Standard algorithms work with iterator ranges. Passing by value lets the function rearrange its copy while preserving the caller’s sequence.

title: Count values matching a condition
prompt: Implement int countNegative(const std::vector<int>& values) using std::count_if and a lambda. At most 1000 elements.
hints: The predicate receives an element and returns whether it should count.
explanation: A lambda defines a small callable at the point of use. count_if applies the predicate to each element and counts true results.

title: Translate an iterator into an index
prompt: Implement int indexOf(const std::vector<int>& values,int target) using std::find. Return the first matching index, or -1. At most 1000 elements.
hints: Compare the iterator with end() before subtracting begin().
explanation: The end iterator is a sentinel one past the last element. It can be compared but must not be dereferenced.

title: Check every element
prompt: Implement bool allEven(const std::vector<int>& values) using std::all_of. Empty input returns true.
hints: Use a predicate testing n % 2 == 0.
explanation: all_of answers whether there is no counterexample. An empty range has no counterexamples and therefore returns true.

title: Capture a comparison value
prompt: Implement int above(const std::vector<int>& values,int threshold) using count_if and a lambda capturing threshold by value. At most 1000 elements.
hints: Write [threshold] as the lambda capture list.
explanation: A value capture stores a copy in the lambda object. The predicate can then use surrounding context while accepting only one element argument.

title: Remove matching elements
prompt: Implement void removeValue(std::vector<int>& values,int target) using C++20 std::erase. Preserve the order of survivors.
hints: std::erase handles both rearrangement and size reduction.
explanation: Removing elements changes the vector’s size. Iterator-based remove alone would only rearrange values; std::erase performs the whole operation.
tests: std::vector<int> v{2,1,2,3}; removeValue(v,2); assert((v==std::vector<int>{1,3})); removeValue(v,9); assert(v.size()==2); std::vector<int> e; removeValue(e,0); assert(e.empty());

title: Sort and remove duplicates
prompt: Implement std::vector<int> uniqueSorted(std::vector<int> values). Return distinct values in ascending order using sort, unique, and erase.
hints: unique returns the new logical end; erase the remaining tail.
explanation: unique only collapses adjacent equal values. Sorting first brings equal values together, then erase reduces the physical size.

title: Transform a collection
prompt: Implement std::vector<int> squares(std::vector<int> values) using std::transform and a lambda. Each element is within -1000..1000.
hints: Use values.begin() as both input and output starting position.
explanation: transform applies a function to each element and writes results through an output iterator. In-place transformation is valid for this unary operation.

title: Search a sorted range
prompt: Implement bool containsSorted(const std::vector<int>& values,int target) using std::binary_search. The input is guaranteed sorted in ascending order.
hints: Do not sort again; rely on the stated precondition.
explanation: Binary search repeatedly halves a sorted search range. Applying it to unsorted input violates its ordering precondition.

title: Keep equal-length names in order
prompt: Implement std::vector<std::string> byLength(std::vector<std::string> values), sorting by increasing length while preserving the relative order of equal-length strings. Use stable_sort.
hints: Compare sizes with <, never <=.
explanation: stable_sort preserves input order among equivalent elements. Its comparison must be strict: comparing a value with itself should return false.
